newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh hoped bomb would spark uprising - witness.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh hoped bomb would spark uprising - witness.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh plotted to blow up the Oklahoma City federal building to avenge the deaths of 80 cult members at Waco and to spark a "general uprising," the star witness in his trial testified on Monday.

Michael Fortier gave the most damning testimony so far against his former army buddy, describing how McVeigh's fury at the 1993 confrontation between federal agents and Branch Davidian cult members at Waco, Texas, led him to plot an attack on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building exactly two years later.

Fortier, 28, said McVeigh and alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols singled out the Oklahoma City federal building for the bombing "because that was where the order for the attack on Waco had come." Nichols will be tried separately later.
McVeigh also wanted to "cause a general uprising," to "knock some people off the fence" and push them into action against the government, Fortier testified.
McVeigh is accused of detonating a huge truck bomb outside the federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people in the worst attack on civilians on U.S. soil.

Fortier has pleaded guilty to four felony counts in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing but did nothing to stop it. He has been in a federal prison for the last 21 months awaiting sentencing. He faces up to 23 years in prison.

His testimony could tie together the different pieces of the government's case against McVeigh but his credibility is expected to come under attack from defence lawyers, who could point out he stands to win a reduced sentence by testifying.
Asked by chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler if he realised he could have stopped the bombing with a phone call, Fortier replied: "I live with that knowledge every day, sir."

Fortier, wearing a brown suit and with his dark hair cut short, seemed nervous as he began his testimony in the hushed courtroom, but grew increasingly confident. McVeigh sometimes scowled during his testimony but otherwise showed little emotion. He nodded his head when Fortier told the court how McVeigh had been the best man at his wedding.

Fortier said McVeigh told him "he had figured out how to make a truck into a bomb" and he described how McVeigh pointed out the target building to him when they both drove to Oklahoma City in late 1994.
Fortier said that initially McVeigh had planned a suicide bombing of the federal building, telling him he planned to stay in the explosives-packed truck to make sure it exploded.
"That's suicide. This is stupid," Fortier recalled telling McVeigh.
He said McVeigh had no feeling for what might happen to innocent people in the bombing.

When Fortier asked McVeigh in 1994 if he was concerned about what might happen to innocent people in an attack on the building, McVeigh said he considered the building's occupants to be like the stormtroopers in the "Star Wars" movies.
The individuals may be innocent but "they were part of the Evil Empire and were guilty by association," Fortier said McVeigh told him.
Fortier testified that, in the months before the bombing, he and McVeigh grew further apart and that McVeigh was berating him for not being willing to help in the bombing.
"I thought it was all falling apart and that him and Terry weren't going to do it," he said.

Fortier served in the army with McVeigh and they shared many of the same far right-wing views. McVeigh often visited Fortier at his Kingman, Arizona home after they left the army and they discussed Waco and the plot to blow up the federal building.

Fortier said he and McVeigh believed the federal government had intentionally attacked the Branch Davidians at Waco and that "potentially they murdered those people." They also thought that "somebody should be held accountable".

Fortier said McVeigh believed the U.S. government had declared war on the American people and feared the United Nations planned a one world government. McVeigh even built a berm around his house to protect it from attack, he said.

The prosecution has called more than 90 witnesses so far, building its case against McVeigh far more rapidly than had been expected. Previous witnesses have linked McVeigh to the rental truck used in the bombing.
